# Vignette: The Sky That Fell

Rangi is a 54-year-old Māori man who has spent the better part of three decades in the cockpit. Flying is not simply what he does — it is, as he once put it quietly during a session, "the only place I ever felt completely myself." That identity now sits at the center of everything he is struggling to hold together.

Three years ago, during a routine training sortie, Rangi experienced a catastrophic dual hydraulic failure at low altitude. The aircraft became unresponsive within seconds. He had perhaps eight seconds to make decisions that most pilots never face in a career. He managed a partial ejection sequence, but the timing was wrong — the seat fired at an angle, and he struck the canopy rail before clearing the aircraft. He remembers a sensation he describes as "being swallowed by noise," and then nothing until he regained consciousness in a field, his left shoulder shattered, two vertebrae fractured, and the aircraft burning three hundred meters away. His co-pilot did not survive.

The physical recovery took fourteen months. The other recovery — the one that brought him here — has not yet begun in any meaningful way, at least not until now.

Rangi returned to limited desk duties within the Air Force after medical clearance, but he has not flown operationally since the accident. His superiors speak of him with respect, and he performs his administrative role competently, but colleagues have noticed he seems elsewhere. He notices it too. He sits through briefings and watches younger pilots receive their assignments, and something in his chest tightens into what he can only call dread — not for them, but for himself, for the version of himself that no longer exists.

At night, the accident replays with a fidelity that waking memory cannot match. He hears the hydraulic warning tone, feels the stick go dead in his hands, and then sees his co-pilot's helmet turning toward him in those last seconds. He wakes rigid, heart hammering, sometimes shouting. His wife, Hinerangi, sleeps lightly now. She reaches for him in the dark and he lets her, though he cannot always feel her touch through whatever has closed around him. He is grateful for her and ashamed of the distance he cannot close.

He avoids the flight line entirely, routing his morning walk to bypass it by nearly a kilometer. He has declined two invitations to attend memorial events for his co-pilot, telling Hinerangi that he is not ready, telling himself the same thing with less conviction each time. When aviation comes up in conversation — at family gatherings, at work functions — he changes the subject or excuses himself. His teenage son, who once dreamed of following his father into the Air Force, has stopped asking about it.

Concentration has become unreliable. Rangi reads the same paragraph multiple times and retains nothing. He sits in meetings and finds himself scanning exits, cataloguing the sounds of the building, alert to nothing in particular and everything at once. He is tired in a way that sleep does not touch. Some mornings he sits in his car in the driveway for twenty minutes before he can make himself go inside.

What he talks about most carefully, as though handling something that might break, is guilt. He has reconstructed those eight seconds hundreds of times, searching for the moment where a different choice might have changed the outcome for his co-pilot. He has not found it, but he has not stopped looking. He carries the man's name — Tama — with a heaviness that he does not share with colleagues and shares only partially with Hinerangi, because he believes, on some level he cannot yet examine directly, that grief is a debt he has not yet finished paying.

He is here now, sitting with his large hands folded in his lap, because Hinerangi asked him to come. He says that is the only reason. But he came back the second week without being asked.
